author: Carlos Martinez
title: Time Trials and Time Attack: Racing Against Yourself in iRacing
description: Master the mental discipline and technical consistency needed to excel in time trials. Learn how to build pace lap-by-lap without traffic interference.

sections.p: Time trials are the purest test in iRacing—no traffic, no defensive racing, just you and the clock. But that simplicity is deceptive. When there's nowhere to hide, every corner becomes a referendum on your braking point, your line, and your mental state. I've spent countless hours grinding time-trial lobbies on my MOZA R9, and I've learned that consistent lap time over 10-15 minutes separates top-tier drivers from the rest. The difference between P1 and P10 often comes down to half a tenth per lap—pure repeatability.

The challenge isn't raw pace. Most drivers can hit their best lap once if conditions align. The real skill is doing it again, and again, without cracking under pressure or losing focus as fatigue sets in. That's what time trials teach you.

sections.h2: Why Time Trials Matter More Than You Think

sections.p: Time trials strip away the chaos of multi-car racing. There's no one to blame for losing positions, no traffic to manage, no contact to worry about. That clarity is uncomfortable—and incredibly valuable. In my experience, drivers who excel at time trials develop a mechanical consistency that translates everywhere: cleaner apexes, more repeatable braking, better muscle memory.

iRacing's time-trial system also rewards progression. You see your own improvement lap-by-lap, and the leaderboard shows exactly where you stand against other drivers running identical conditions. For someone trying to climb the ranking or qualify for competitive leagues, time trials are non-negotiable. They're also low-stakes for practice—no incident points, no SR damage, just data.

list: Pure consistency metric: every lap is your own baseline, no external variables
Pressure-free grinding: practice without SR or incident-point consequences
Leaderboard transparency: see exactly where you rank and by how much
Mental discipline building: learn to stay sharp over 10+ laps at limit
Setup tuning feedback: immediate, direct correlation between change and lap time

sections.h2: Building a Time-Trial Session That Works

sections.p: The best time-trial prep mirrors qualifying preparation, but with a longer mindset. I spend the first 3-4 laps getting heat into my tires and settling into the rhythm. My MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals help here—I'm checking brake consistency lap-to-lap, making sure I'm hitting the same pressure point in each corner. Then I'll do 5-7 hot laps in sequence, looking for the run where everything clicks.

The key is not chasing one perfect lap, but chaining together a sequence of strong ones. Time-trial standings often use your best single lap, but some events—especially longer formats—average your top three laps or require you to set your time over a fixed session length. Know the rules going in.

olist: Arrive early and run 2-3 laps cold to warm brakes, tires, and your hands
Settle into a rhythm: focus on repeatability, not aggression
Mark your best lap and rewatch the telemetry (check apex speed, throttle application, brake points)
Run 5-7 consecutive hot laps without pause—this is where fatigue and pressure reveal cracks
If you improve, keep pushing; if you plateau or get nervous, step back and review

sections.tip: Don't chase the one perfect lap. Time trials test your ability to produce consistent, fast laps in sequence. A 1:23.2 done three times in a row beats a 1:23.0 followed by two 1:23.8s.

sections.h2: Technical Setup Adjustments for Time-Trial Pace

sections.p: Time trials expose setup weaknesses quickly because you're running the same lines hundreds of times. Small changes in brake bias, anti-roll-bar stiffness, or differential lock can mean 0.1–0.3 seconds per lap. I always start with a baseline setup from the car folder or a trusted setup shop, then make only one change at a time and test for 2-3 laps before moving to the next tweak.

Focus your setup work on consistency, not outright speed. A setup that's slightly loose but forgiving will yield faster lap times in a 10-lap sequence than one that's on the edge and punishes mistakes. My MOZA R9 wheelbase—~9 N·m of peak torque—gives me clear feedback about how the car is responding, so I can feel when a change has helped or hurt stability.

list: Brake bias: aim for zero lock-up at your hardest braking points; adjust 0.5–1% at a time
Differential lock: increase on-throttle lock if the car understeers exiting corners
Suspension stiffness: softer (lower numbers) typically aids consistency; stiffer helps committed drivers
Tire pressure: start with baseline and adjust ±0.5 psi per run; monitor tire temps for trends
Downforce: lower = more speed but less stable; higher = more forgiving but slower

sections.h2: The Mental Game: Staying Focused Over Distance

sections.p: Here's what separates top-10 time-trial finishers from the pack: mental discipline. After 8–10 laps at the absolute limit, fatigue creeps in. Your eyes feel heavy, your fingers tense up on the wheel, and that last critical turn—the one you nailed perfectly on laps 3, 5, and 7—suddenly feels uncertain. That's where focus breaks and lap time bleeds away.

I battle this by treating each lap like a separate event. Between runs, I take a breath, reset my hands on my wheel, and review the previous lap in my head: did I hit the apex in turn 4? Was my throttle application smooth? I don't carry frustration or overconfidence from one lap to the next. It sounds simple, but it's harder than it sounds when you're tired and hungry for that next tenth.

list: Take a reset breath between laps—step back from the wheel mentally for 10 seconds
Review the last lap logically: one key moment where you could improve, nothing more
Don't chase mistakes: if you made a small error 3 laps ago, let it go and focus on the next run
Stay hydrated: have water nearby and sip between sessions, not during
Time your sessions: run when you're alert, not after hours of grinding other series

sections.h2: Using Telemetry to Close the Gap

sections.p: iRacing's replay and telemetry tools are your secret weapon. After a time-trial run, I always compare my best lap against the leaderboard leaders if their replay is available. I watch their throttle application in corner exits, their braking points, their line through high-speed corners. Then I load my own telemetry and look for the moments where I'm losing time—usually it's 0.05–0.15 seconds spread across 3-4 corners, not one catastrophic mistake.

The telemetry overlay in iRacing's replay shows you throttle %, brake %, steering angle, and speed all overlaid on a visual line. I use this to spot inconsistencies: am I lifting to different speeds in turn 7 each lap? Is my apex speed varying by more than 2 mph? Small variations compound over a lap, and telemetry makes them visible.

sections.tip: Compare your best lap against a top-10 leaderboard driver lap-by-lap. You'll often find that the difference is 0.02–0.05 seconds in one specific corner, not a fundamental skill gap across the whole track.

sections.h2: Time Attack: The Format That Rewards Bravery

sections.p: Time attack is a variant where drivers get a fixed number of runs (often 3-5) and only their single best lap counts. This format rewards bravery in a way that standard time trials don't. You're not chaining together 10 clean laps; you're trying to extract one perfect lap knowing you have limited attempts. The mental calculus is different: do you push harder on run 2 and risk a spin, or do you treat run 2 as a practice warm-up and go all-in on run 3?

My approach is conservative early. Runs 1 and 2 get me fully dialed in and heat into the tires, then I commit fully on run 3. If I make a mistake on run 3, I have runs 4 and 5 as safety nets. This reduces the pressure on any single lap and often means my best lap comes when I'm most comfortable, not most desperate.

The best drivers I've raced against use time trials as a grinding tool: they'll enter the same time-trial lobby every week and chase incremental improvement. Over 4-6 weeks, a 0.2-second improvement—from 1:23.5 to 1:23.3—is huge. That's not luck or a setup change; that's pure muscle memory and familiarity.

If you're serious about climbing iRacing's rankings, dedicate one hour per week to time trials on your target track. Treat it as skill development, not entertainment. Track your best lap each week, review telemetry religiously, and adjust your approach based on what you find. Within a month, you'll see measurable progress—and more importantly, you'll develop the consistency that transfers to multi-car racing.

list: Pick one track and commit to weekly time-trial sessions for 4-6 weeks minimum
Keep a spreadsheet of your best lap, date, and setup—look for what works
Watch top-leaderboard drivers and note their lines, especially in corners where you lose time
Focus on one corner per session: pick the turn you're weakest in and drill it until it's smooth
Join a time-trial focused league or community to add accountability and friendly competition

faqs.q: What's the difference between a time trial and time attack in iRacing?
faqs.a: Time trials give you a full session duration (usually 15-30 minutes) to set your best single lap, usually with multiple attempts. Time attack gives you a limited number of runs (3-5) and only your single fastest lap counts. Time attack is more high-pressure and reward bravery; time trials reward consistency over a longer session.

faqs.q: How do I stop making mistakes in the last few laps of a time-trial run?
faqs.a: Fatigue and pressure cause errors late in a sequence. Combat this by taking a mental reset between laps—step back from the wheel, breathe, and treat each lap as a fresh start. Stay hydrated, don't rush, and remember that a solid 1:23.2 is better than chasing a 1:23.0 and losing focus. Mental discipline beats raw talent in long time-trial sessions.

faqs.q: Should I adjust my setup before a time trial, or just drive what I have?
faqs.a: Start with a proven baseline setup to avoid wasting time chasing setup rabbitholes. Make one small adjustment at a time and test it for 2-3 laps. Most lap-time gains come from consistency and driver precision, not setup tweaks. Setup matters, but consistency matters more. Focus on repeatability first, then optimize once you're comfortable.

faqs.q: How do I know if I'm actually improving or just having a good day?
faqs.a: Track your best lap each week and average your top three laps over a session. If your average is improving by 0.1+ seconds over 4-6 weeks, that's real improvement. A one-off fast lap might be luck or perfect conditions. Consistency across multiple laps—and consistency across multiple weeks—is the true measure of progress.
